title: Your nearest mosque
hookLine: every mosque is linked to the first

lines: A DOME, A SHOP, A BASEMENT ROOM.
A NICHE ON THE FRONT WALL.
cards: Somewhere near you there may well be a mosque. It might have a dome. It might be a converted shop with a hand-painted sign, a room above a pharmacy, a prayer space in a hospital basement or a university hallway.
You may have walked past it without looking up. Inside, on the front wall, there's very likely a small arched niche, or just a mark, showing which way to face. That mark is a thread.
Pull it, and it runs across roads, seas and deserts to one house in Mecca. Today, the last of our houses of prayer: your nearest mosque.

teach.b: First, the thread. The niche is the mihrab, and the direction it shows is the qibla, toward the Ka'ba. The Qur'an tells believers that wherever they are, they turn their faces toward the Sacred Mosque in prayer.
So the smallest prayer room and the grandest hall point the same way. Second, the first house.

Five days ago we heard the Qur'an call the house at Becca "the first Sanctuary appointed for mankind." A shop-front prayer room in a city you've never seen is turned toward that same house: linked to the first.

A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says whoever enters a mosque should pray two units of prayer before sitting down, a greeting for the house itself. Visitors who aren't Muslim aren't asked to pray, of course.
Shoes come off at the door, people dress modestly, and a quiet hello goes a long way. Some mosques hold open days and welcome questions. Fourth, the blessing.

Four days ago, in Medina, we heard the verse asking believers to send blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Those blessings are called salawat, and some Muslims say them as they step into a mosque.
Now look back. This long stretch walked through history and civilization: caliphs and scholars, libraries and soup kitchens, empires, colonial rule, migration, and these houses of prayer.
Mecca, Medina, Jerusalem, mud and wood, Jakarta and Abu Dhabi, and the one down your street. Next comes a new camp: the holy days in history.

how: Muslims pray in the nearest mosque when they can, especially for Friday prayer, facing the mihrab toward Mecca; some mosques also welcome visitors and hold open days.

o: the greeting prayer on entering a mosque
the arched niche set in a mosque's front wall
the direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba

p: the niche on the front wall

games.q: you're a Muslim walking into a mosque before the congregation has gathered. what does the hadith ask you to do before you sit?
o: sit straight down and wait quietly.
pray two units of prayer, a greeting for the house.
walk to the front and touch the mihrab.
games.why: the hadith in Bukhari asks for two units of prayer before sitting, a greeting for the mosque itself.

practice: Picture your nearest mosque, or the streets where one might be, and stand across the road in your mind, watching the door: someone early, someone late, someone holding a child's hand.
If you pray, send salawat on the Prophet in the words you know, once for each person who goes in; if not, simply wish that house and its people well.

wordCard.voice: Qibla, the direction of prayer toward the Ka'ba, that every mosque's mihrab, however small or grand, points its worshippers to face. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the direction of prayer, toward the Ka'ba in Mecca.

carryVoice: Your line: linked to the first. Every mihrab, however small, points to the same house. Until tomorrow.
